entries.meaning: To make something begin or become active in a hurry. ---
examples: A small grant can kickstart a business.
That one interview kickstarted her career.
The city is kickstarting the season with a free concert.
entries.contrast: Often written with a hyphen: kick-start.

entries.meaning: To hit someone with your knee. ---
examples: The coach warned them never to knee an opponent.
She kneed him in the thigh going for the rebound.
He was kneed twice before the referee stepped in.
entries.contrast: The k is silent, and the past kneed sounds exactly like need.

entries.meaning: To stab or cut someone with a knife. ---
examples: Two men tried to knife him outside the bar.
Someone knifed the tires on every car in the lot.
He was knifed in the arm during the robbery.
entries.contrast: The noun makes the plural knives, but the verb takes a plain -s: he knifes.

entries.meaning: To give someone the rank of knight in a formal ceremony. ---
examples: British monarchs knight actors, athletes and scientists.
The queen knighted him in 1965.
She was knighted for her work in medicine.
entries.русский: посвящать в рыцари, посвятить в рыцари
entries.contrast: The k is silent: knight sounds exactly like night.

entries.meaning: To behave in an excessively obedient way toward someone powerful. ---
examples: She refuses to kowtow to the board.
The paper kowtowed to its advertisers for years.
Critics accused the mayor of kowtowing to developers.
entries.contrast: Both syllables rhyme with now, not with know, and the verb takes to.

entries.meaning: To work hard at something slow and difficult. ---
examples: Crews labor through the night after every storm.
He labored over that speech for a week.
The old engine was laboring on the last hill.
entries.contrast: American spelling is labor, labored; British writing uses labour, laboured.

entries.meaning: To cut or tear skin deeply and roughly. ---
examples: Broken glass can lacerate a hand in an instant.
The fall lacerated his knee.
She came in with a lacerated scalp.

entries.meaning: To coat wood or metal with a hard glossy varnish. ---
examples: They lacquer each box by hand.
He sanded and lacquered the tabletop over the weekend.
A lacquered red tray sat by the register.

entries.meaning: To serve liquid food with a large deep spoon. ---
examples: Ladle the soup into warm bowls.
Volunteers ladled stew for four hundred people.
She stood at the pot, ladling chili onto rice.

entries.meaning: To criticize someone or something harshly and in public. ---
examples: Columnists lambaste the plan every other week.
The coach lambasted his defense after the loss.
She was lambasted online for one careless remark.
entries.contrast: Also spelled lambast; either way the stress falls on the second syllable.

entries.meaning: To express deep sorrow or regret about something. ---
examples: Older residents lament the loss of the corner store.
He lamented that nobody reads the local paper anymore.
Critics have long lamented the state of the building.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (they lament the loss of the theater), intransitive (the whole town gathered to lament)

entries.meaning: To cover something with a thin protective layer, or to build it up out of thin layers. ---
examples: They laminate every ID card at the front desk.
I laminated the recipe so it would survive the kitchen.
The counter is laminated to look like marble.
entries.contrast: The verb ends LAM-uh-nayt; the noun and adjective end LAM-uh-nuht.

entries.meaning: To mock someone publicly with humor, especially in writing or a sketch. ---
examples: Late-night shows lampoon every candidate in turn.
The cartoon lampooned the mayor's new haircut.
He has been lampooned on television for twenty years.

entries.meaning: To be left somewhere in a bad or forgotten state for a long time. ---
examples: Bills can languish in committee for years.
The proposal languished on someone's desk all summer.
Thousands of cases are still languishing in the courts.

entries.meaning: To fasten something with a small bar or catch. ---
examples: Please latch the gate behind you.
He latched the screen door and turned off the porch light.
The window has not been latching properly since the storm.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (latch the gate), intransitive (the door will not latch)
entries.contrast: The third person adds -es: it latches.

entries.meaning: To praise someone or something highly, usually in public. ---
examples: Critics laud the film for its honesty.
The mayor lauded the firefighters by name.
She has been widely lauded for the research.
entries.contrast: Laud (LAWD, to praise) is not loud (LOWD).

entries.meaning: To make the sounds and the face that show you find something funny. ---
examples: Babies laugh before they can talk.
Everyone laughed when the microphone squealed.
She was laughing so hard she had to sit down.
entries.contrast: The gh is pronounced /f/: LAF, and the past is LAFT.

entries.meaning: To give something very generously, even excessively, to someone. ---
examples: Grandparents lavish attention on the youngest child.
The company lavished bonuses on its sales team.
He has been lavishing gifts on her since June.
entries.contrast: The verb takes on: lavish praise on someone.

entries.meaning: To drain away through soil or another material, or to wash something away that way. ---
examples: Heavy rain leaches nitrogen out of the topsoil.
Lead leached into the drinking water for months.
Old pipes are still leaching metal into the supply.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (rain leaches nutrients out of the soil), intransitive (chemicals leached into the creek)
entries.contrast: Leach sounds exactly like leech, the blood-sucking worm.

entries.meaning: To jump ahead of others, skipping the usual steps in between. ---
examples: Cheap solar let some countries leapfrog the power grid entirely.
She leapfrogged two colleagues to become director.
The company is leapfrogging a whole generation of hardware.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the phone leapfrogged its rivals), intransitive (the kids leapfrog across the lawn)
entries.contrast: The g doubles: leapfrogged, leapfrogging.

entries.meaning: To look at someone in an unpleasant, openly sexual way. ---
examples: Men at the back table leer at every waitress.
He leered at her across the bar.
She caught him leering and moved seats.
entries.contrast: The verb takes at: leer at someone.

entries.meaning: To make something seem lawful, acceptable, or respectable. ---
examples: Coverage like that can legitimize fringe ideas.
The election legitimized the new government.
Critics say the award is legitimizing very bad science.
entries.contrast: American spelling is legitimize; British writing uses legitimise.

entries.meaning: To use something you already have in order to gain a further advantage. ---
examples: Small firms leverage social media to reach customers.
She leveraged her contacts into a much better job.
They are leveraging the brand to sell insurance.

entries.meaning: To rise and float in the air with no visible support. ---
examples: Magicians appear to levitate a foot above the stage.
He levitated a coin above his open palm.
Dust hung in the beam of light, levitating there for a minute.
entries.русский: левитировать, парить в воздухе; поднимать в воздух
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the magician levitated his assistant), intransitive (the table seemed to levitate)

entries.meaning: To make laws, rules, or an economy less strict and more open. ---
examples: Several states plan to liberalize their liquor laws.
The country liberalized trade in the 1990s.
Banking has been steadily liberalized since then.
entries.contrast: American spelling is liberalize; British writing uses liberalise.

entries.meaning: To say that one thing is similar to another. ---
examples: Coaches often liken a season to a marathon.
She likened the debate to a food fight.
His style has been likened to early Hemingway.
entries.contrast: The verb always takes to: liken one thing to another.

entries.meaning: To be alive, or to have your home in a particular place. ---
examples: Both my sisters live in Chicago.
He lived alone in that house for thirty years.
They have been living out of suitcases since May.
entries.contrast: The verb is LIV, rhyming with give; the adjective in a live broadcast is LYV.

entries.meaning: To limit something to one area, or to adapt a product for a particular country. ---
examples: Doctors could not localize the source of the pain.
The studio localized the game for eleven markets.
The outbreak has been localized to two counties.
entries.русский: локализовать, определять местоположение; адаптировать под рынок
entries.contrast: American spelling is localize; British writing uses localise.

entries.meaning: To stand or wait around in a place with no clear purpose. ---
examples: Signs ask people not to loiter near the entrance.
Teenagers loitered outside the theater until midnight.
He was stopped for loitering in the parking garage.

entries.meaning: To turn your eyes toward something, or to seem a certain way. ---
examples: Look both ways before you cross.
She looked tired the whole week.
He was looking straight at the camera.
entries.contrast: Look is about directing your eyes; see is about what your eyes take in, and watch is about following something over time.

entries.meaning: To sit or lie in a relaxed, lazy way. ---
examples: On Sundays they lounge by the pool all afternoon.
He lounged on the couch with the game on.
Guests were lounging in the shade when we arrived.

entries.meaning: To offer or quote a price far below what something is really worth. ---
examples: Dealers routinely lowball customers on trade-ins.
The insurer lowballed her claim by half.
We walked away after being lowballed twice.
entries.русский: занижать, занизить (цену, оценку); предлагать заниженную цену

entries.meaning: To put oil or grease on moving parts so that they slide easily. ---
examples: Technicians lubricate the bearings every six months.
He lubricated the chain before the ride.
The gears had not been lubricated in years.

entries.meaning: To carry or drag something heavy with a lot of effort. ---
examples: I have to lug these boxes up three flights of stairs.
She lugged her suitcase across the whole terminal.
We spent the morning lugging firewood to the cabin.
entries.contrast: One syllable ending in a single consonant, so the g doubles: lugged, lugging.

entries.meaning: To move forward slowly and heavily, as if too big to be graceful. ---
examples: Loaded trucks lumber up the hill in the slow lane.
A bear lumbered across the road in front of us.
The old bus came lumbering around the corner.
entries.contrast: The noun lumber means sawn wood; the verb has nothing to do with it.

entries.meaning: To put different people or things into one group as if they were all the same. ---
examples: Don't lump every teenager into one category.
The report lumped salaries and bonuses into a single line.
Freelancers are often lumped in with part-time staff.
entries.русский: сваливать в одну кучу, объединять; свалить

entries.meaning: To make a sudden, uncontrolled movement forward or to one side. ---
examples: Old ferries lurch whenever a big wave hits.
The train lurched and coffee went everywhere.
The country has been lurching from one crisis to the next.

entries.meaning: To attract someone somewhere by offering something tempting. ---
examples: Low prices lure shoppers into the store.
The ad lured thousands of applicants.
Investors were lured by promises of quick returns.

entries.meaning: To wait somewhere quietly and out of sight, often with bad intentions. ---
examples: Predators lurk in the shallow water near the reef.
Someone lurked outside the building for an hour.
Doubts were still lurking at the back of her mind.

entries.meaning: To feel a very strong desire for someone or something. ---
examples: Collectors lust after cars they will never drive.
He lusted for the corner office for years.
She has been lusting after that guitar since high school.
entries.contrast: Lust needs after or for: you lust after a car, never lust a car.

entries.meaning: For a mob to kill someone, especially by hanging, without any trial. ---
examples: The crowd threatened to lynch the prisoner.
Thousands of Black Americans were lynched between 1880 and 1950.
Newspapers of the era described mobs lynching men with no evidence against them.

entries.meaning: To make someone extremely angry or irritated. ---
examples: Small delays madden him more than big ones.
The constant noise maddened everyone in the office.
It is maddening to lose a file you never saved.

entries.meaning: To make a piece of metal behave like a magnet. ---
examples: A strong current will magnetize the iron core.
He magnetized the screwdriver so the screws would stick to it.
The strip on a hotel key card is magnetized.
entries.contrast: American spelling is magnetize; British writing uses magnetise.

entries.meaning: To injure someone so badly that part of the body is permanently damaged. ---
examples: Landmines still maim farmers decades after a war ends.
The blast maimed three workers.
He was maimed in a factory accident at nineteen.

entries.meaning: To say cruel and untrue things about someone or something. ---
examples: Rivals malign each other every campaign season.
The press maligned her long before the trial began.
Carbohydrates may be the most maligned nutrient in America.
entries.contrast: The g is silent: muh-LYN, and the same spelling is also an adjective, as in a malign influence.

entries.meaning: To be present at a post or piece of equipment in order to operate it. ---
examples: Volunteers man the phones during the fundraiser.
Two officers manned the checkpoint all night.
The booth was manned by students from the college.
entries.contrast: The n doubles: manned, manning.

entries.meaning: To require something officially by law or by rule. ---
examples: Several states mandate paid sick leave.
The court mandated a full recount.
Masks were mandated in hospitals that winter.

entries.meaning: To damage something badly by crushing, twisting, or tearing it. ---
examples: Cheap printers mangle thick paper.
The crash mangled the front of the car.
Her name is always mangled by people reading it aloud.

entries.meaning: To move or push a person or object roughly, using force. ---
examples: Please don't manhandle the equipment.
Security manhandled the protester into the street.
She complained of being manhandled by the guards.

entries.meaning: To trim and care for the fingernails, or to trim something so that it looks perfectly neat. ---
examples: The salon can manicure your nails in twenty minutes.
He manicured the hedge into a straight green wall.
The resort is surrounded by manicured lawns.

entries.meaning: To show something clearly, or for something hidden to become visible. ---
examples: Stress can manifest as headaches and poor sleep.
The illness manifested itself only after several months.
Symptoms are manifesting earlier than doctors expected.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the patient manifested no symptoms), intransitive (the fault manifested in the second year)

entries.meaning: For a man to explain something to a woman in a condescending way, assuming she does not already know it. ---
examples: Please don't mansplain my own research to me.
He mansplained the offside rule to a former referee.
She walked off rather than listen to him mansplaining again.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (he mansplained the rules to her), intransitive (stop mansplaining)

entries.meaning: To make a map of an area, or to record in detail how something is arranged. ---
examples: Satellites map the ocean floor from orbit.
Researchers mapped the human genome by 2003.
The coastline has been mapped in extraordinary detail.
entries.русский: наносить на карту, составлять карту; картировать
entries.contrast: The p doubles: mapped, mapping.

entries.meaning: To spoil the appearance or the quality of something. ---
examples: Deep scratches mar the finish on the table.
Protests marred the opening ceremony.
The election was marred by accusations of fraud.
entries.contrast: The r doubles: marred, marring.

entries.meaning: To treat a person or group as unimportant and push them to the edge of a society or a discussion. ---
examples: Bad policy can marginalize whole neighborhoods.
The new rules marginalized the smaller parties.
She writes about communities that have been marginalized for generations.
entries.contrast: American spelling is marginalize; British writing uses marginalise.

entries.meaning: To leave someone in a place they have no way of getting away from. ---
examples: A storm like that can maroon hikers for days.
The snow marooned us at the airport overnight.
Passengers were marooned on the ship for a week.
entries.русский: бросать на произвол судьбы, высаживать (на необитаемом острове)

entries.meaning: To gather people, facts, or resources and organize them for a purpose. ---
examples: A good lawyer knows how to marshal evidence.
She marshaled support from three separate committees.
Every available crew was marshaled to fight the fire.
entries.contrast: American English keeps one l: marshaled, marshaling; British English doubles it. The homophone martial means military.

entries.meaning: To pretend to be something or someone that you are not. ---
examples: Plenty of ads masquerade as news articles.
He masqueraded as a doctor for two years.
The charge was masquerading as a routine service fee.
entries.contrast: It takes as: you masquerade as a doctor.

entries.meaning: To plan and direct a complicated operation, especially a crime or a campaign. ---
examples: Nobody knows who masterminds these attacks.
He masterminded the biggest bank robbery in state history.
The merger was masterminded by two junior analysts.

entries.meaning: To become real and actually happen, or to appear suddenly out of nowhere. ---
examples: The promised funding never seems to materialize.
A waiter materialized beside our table.
The recession everyone feared has not materialized.

entries.meaning: To enroll formally as a student at a college or university. ---
examples: Students who matriculate in August graduate in May.
He matriculated at Michigan in 1998.
Fewer transfer students are matriculating this year.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the college matriculated 900 freshmen), intransitive (she matriculated in the fall)

entries.meaning: To be important or to make a real difference. ---
examples: Small details matter more than people think.
Nothing else mattered to him that day.
Money has never mattered much to her.

entries.meaning: To attack and wound someone badly, usually said of an animal. ---
examples: Bears rarely maul people who keep their distance.
A dog mauled a child in the park last summer.
He was mauled by a mountain lion and survived.
entries.contrast: Maul and mall sound exactly the same in American English.

entries.meaning: To replace human or animal labor with machines. ---
examples: Cheap robots let small farms mechanize the harvest.
The army mechanized its infantry in the 1930s.
Sorting has been almost completely mechanized.

entries.meaning: To sit quietly and focus the mind, for calm or for religious reasons. ---
examples: I meditate for ten minutes before work.
She meditated every morning for a year.
He was meditating when the phone rang.
entries.contrast: To think deeply about a topic is to meditate on it.

entries.meaning: To blend two or more things into one, or to blend together. ---
examples: Good producers meld several styles into one sound.
The two departments melded within a month.
The flavors keep melding as the stew sits overnight.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the album melds jazz and hip-hop), intransitive (the two teams melded quickly)

entries.meaning: To become calmer and less harsh, or to make someone that way. ---
examples: A few years in the job will mellow anyone.
Fatherhood mellowed him considerably.
The wine is still mellowing in oak barrels.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (age mellowed him), intransitive (he has mellowed a lot)

entries.meaning: To do something that keeps the memory of a person or an event alive. ---
examples: Cities memorialize their dead with statues and street names.
The quilt memorialized thousands of victims.
That night is memorialized on a plaque beside the door.

entries.meaning: To threaten someone or something with harm. ---
examples: Wildfires menace the same canyon every summer.
Two stray dogs menaced the mail carrier.
A menacing figure stood at the end of the hall.

entries.meaning: To have the monthly bleeding that comes from the uterus. ---
examples: Most girls begin to menstruate between ten and fifteen.
She had not menstruated for three months.
Athletes who train very hard sometimes stop menstruating.

entries.meaning: To make the crying sound that a cat makes. ---
examples: Cats meow at humans and almost never at each other.
The kitten meowed until someone fed it.
Something was meowing under the porch all night.
entries.contrast: American spelling is meow; miaow is British.

entries.meaning: To deserve serious attention, praise, or treatment. ---
examples: Few emails merit an immediate reply.
The proposal merited a longer discussion than it got.
Her work has merited every award it received.
entries.contrast: The stress is on the first syllable, so the t does not double: merited, meriting.

entries.meaning: To fit or work together well, or to make two things fit together. ---
examples: Their working styles mesh surprisingly well.
The new software never meshed with the old database.
We are still meshing the two teams into one.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (mesh the two schedules), intransitive (their styles mesh well)

entries.meaning: To break down food, medicine, or another substance in the body and turn it into energy. ---
examples: Children metabolize caffeine far more slowly than adults.
His liver metabolized the drug in under an hour.
Alcohol is metabolized at a fixed rate no matter what you eat.

entries.meaning: For a cancer to spread from its original site to other parts of the body, or for a problem to spread out of control. ---
examples: Some tumors metastasize within months.
The scandal metastasized into a full federal investigation.
By then the cancer had metastasized to her spine.

entries.meaning: To control every small detail of someone else's work, usually far too closely. ---
examples: Good managers delegate; bad ones micromanage.
He micromanaged the project until half the team quit.
Nobody enjoys being micromanaged.
entries.русский: контролировать каждую мелочь, вмешиваться в мелочи
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (she micromanages her staff), intransitive (he cannot stop micromanaging)

entries.meaning: To fill a place or an organization with soldiers and military equipment, or to give it a military character. ---
examples: Both sides continue to militarize the border.
The government militarized the islands in the 1990s.
Critics say local police have been steadily militarized.

entries.meaning: To be a strong reason why something does not happen or is not true. ---
examples: Several factors militate against an early release.
His age militated against him throughout the hiring process.
Everything about the site was militating against a quick build.
entries.contrast: Militate takes against and means "work against". Do not confuse it with mitigate, which means "make less severe".

entries.meaning: To dig valuable material out of the ground, or to search through something for what is useful in it. ---
examples: Three companies mine lithium in that valley.
They mined coal there for eighty years.
Historians have mined the archive for new material.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (they mine copper here), intransitive (the company mines for lithium)

entries.meaning: To make a much smaller version of a device or a machine. ---
examples: Engineers keep trying to miniaturize the battery.
The company miniaturized the sensor until it fit inside a watch.
Hearing aids have been enormously miniaturized since the 1980s.

entries.meaning: To take a second, smaller field of study at an American college. ---
examples: You can minor in Spanish and still finish on time.
She majored in biology and minored in music.
He is minoring in computer science.
entries.contrast: Minor in is the smaller field, major in the main one. Both need in.

entries.meaning: To make coins officially, or to create something brand new. ---
examples: The government still mints pennies at a loss.
They minted a special coin for the anniversary.
Silicon Valley has minted a great many young millionaires.

entries.meaning: To get someone or something stuck in a difficult situation they cannot easily escape. ---
examples: Lawsuits can mire a company for years.
Heavy rain mired the trucks in mud.
The bill is still mired in committee.
entries.contrast: It is nearly always passive: be mired in debt, in mud, in scandal.

entries.meaning: To put something out of its correct position in relation to something else. ---
examples: One loose screw can misalign the whole mechanism.
The printer misaligned every page in the batch.
Their incentives are badly misaligned with ours.

entries.meaning: To use a rule, a method, or money in the wrong way or for the wrong purpose. ---
examples: Judges sometimes misapply a statute written for another era.
The clinic misapplied the grant money.
The term is constantly misapplied in the press.
entries.русский: неправильно применять, применять не по назначению; неправильно применить
entries.contrast: The y becomes ie: misapplies, misapplied, but misapplying.

entries.meaning: To make a mistake in working something out, or to judge a situation wrongly. ---
examples: It is easy to miscalculate how long a move will take.
She miscalculated the tax by a thousand dollars.
They had badly miscalculated the public reaction.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (he miscalculated the dose), intransitive (the general badly miscalculated)

entries.meaning: To lose a pregnancy before the baby could survive, or, of a plan or of justice, to fail. ---
examples: Many women who miscarry never learn why.
She miscarried at eleven weeks.
Justice has plainly miscarried in this case.
entries.русский: иметь выкидыш, потерять ребёнка; терпеть неудачу
entries.contrast: The y becomes ie: miscarries, miscarried, but miscarrying.

entries.meaning: To put something or someone into the wrong category. ---
examples: Companies often misclassify employees as contractors.
The lab misclassified the sample.
Thousands of drivers were misclassified and lost their benefits.
entries.русский: неверно классифицировать, ошибочно относить к категории

entries.meaning: To understand a statement or an action in the wrong way. ---
examples: People often misconstrue silence as agreement.
He misconstrued her politeness as interest.
The remark was widely misconstrued.
entries.русский: неверно истолковывать, превратно понимать; истолковать неверно

entries.meaning: To identify an illness or a problem wrongly. ---
examples: Doctors sometimes misdiagnose a heart attack as indigestion.
The clinic misdiagnosed her for two years.
He was misdiagnosed with asthma as a child.
entries.русский: ставить неверный диагноз; поставить неверный диагноз

entries.meaning: To send something or someone the wrong way, or to lead attention away from the truth. ---
examples: A single wrong digit can misdirect a payment.
The mailroom misdirected the package to Ohio.
Voters felt they were being misdirected by the ads.
entries.русский: направлять не туда, вводить в заблуждение; направить неверно

entries.meaning: For a gun, an engine, or a plan to fail to work the way it should. ---
examples: Old engines misfire on cold mornings.
The joke misfired badly.
Every attempt at an apology has misfired.
entries.русский: давать осечку, не срабатывать; дать осечку

entries.meaning: To lead someone to a wrong belief or a wrong course of action. ---
examples: Bad data can misguide an entire department.
The brochure misguided buyers about the fees.
It was a well-meant but misguided attempt to help.
entries.русский: вводить в заблуждение, направлять по ложному пути

entries.meaning: To deal with a situation badly, or to handle an object carelessly. ---
examples: Airlines mishandle about six bags per thousand.
The department mishandled the investigation from the start.
Evidence that has been mishandled is useless in court.
entries.русский: неправильно обращаться, плохо справляться; допустить ошибку

entries.meaning: To decide wrongly who or what someone or something is. ---
examples: Witnesses misidentify suspects more often than juries assume.
The app misidentified the mushroom as edible.
He had been misidentified in the photo caption.
entries.русский: неверно опознавать, ошибочно определять; неверно опознать

entries.meaning: To give someone information that is wrong, whether on purpose or not. ---
examples: Careless headlines misinform more people than outright lies do.
The agent misinformed us about the deadline.
Voters had been deliberately misinformed.

entries.meaning: To understand something in a way that is not correct. ---
examples: It is easy to misinterpret a short text message.
He misinterpreted the chart completely.
Her silence was being misinterpreted as approval.
entries.русский: неверно истолковывать, превратно понимать; неверно истолковать

entries.meaning: To form a wrong opinion about a person, a distance, or a situation. ---
examples: Drivers routinely misjudge how far away a cyclist is.
I misjudged him badly.
The mood of the country had been misjudged by everyone.

entries.meaning: To put the wrong name or label on something, or to describe someone wrongly. ---
examples: Stores sometimes mislabel farmed fish as wild.
The pharmacy mislabeled the bottle.
Plenty of these kids are mislabeled as lazy.
entries.русский: неверно маркировать, навешивать неверный ярлык; неверно обозначить
entries.contrast: American English keeps one l: mislabeled, mislabeling; British English doubles it.

entries.meaning: To run or handle something badly, especially money, a business, or a crisis. ---
examples: Boards that mismanage their reserves rarely survive a downturn.
Auditors found the charity had mismanaged donations for years.
The mayor was accused of mismanaging the flood response.

entries.meaning: To put together two things that do not suit or correspond to each other. ---
examples: The system will mismatch records whenever two customers share a birthday.
Someone mismatched the sizes, so half the shirts went back.
The two fighters were badly mismatched from the opening bell.
entries.contrast: The noun is stressed on the first syllable, MIS-match; the verb on the second, mis-MATCH.

entries.meaning: To put something somewhere and then be unable to find it. ---
examples: I always misplace my keys when I am in a hurry.
She misplaced the paperwork somewhere in the office.
The file has been misplaced, not deleted.
entries.русский: класть не на место, терять; затерять

entries.meaning: To print something incorrectly, so that the text or the figures come out wrong. ---
examples: Newspapers sometimes misprint a date and no one notices for days.
The program misprinted her name in the cast list.
The address was misprinted on every flyer we handed out.
entries.русский: печатать с ошибкой, напечатать с опечаткой
entries.contrast: The noun is stressed on the first syllable, MIS-print; the verb on the second, mis-PRINT.

entries.meaning: To describe someone or something falsely, so that people get the wrong idea. ---
examples: Advertising must not misrepresent what a product actually does.
He misrepresented his income on the loan application.
She felt her position had been misrepresented in the article.
entries.русский: искажать, представлять в ложном свете; исказить

entries.meaning: To say or write something inaccurately, by mistake or on purpose. ---
examples: Witnesses often misstate the time of an event.
The senator misstated the number of jobs the plant created.
The company has misstated its earnings for two quarters running.
entries.contrast: Keep both s's: mis + state gives misstate, misstated.

entries.meaning: To use something in the wrong way or for the wrong purpose. ---
examples: Never misuse a company card for personal expenses.
He misused money that had been set aside for repairs.
The word is constantly misused online.
entries.contrast: The verb ends in a /z/ sound, mis-YOOZ; the noun misuse ends in /s/, mis-YOOS.

entries.meaning: To crowd around someone or something in a large, excited group. ---
examples: Fans mob the players every time the team lands.
Reporters mobbed her outside the courthouse.
The store was mobbed on the first morning of the sale.
entries.contrast: A single final consonant after a short vowel doubles: mob → mobbed, mobbing.

entries.meaning: To adjust something so that it changes in a controlled way, especially the tone or strength of a voice or a signal. ---
examples: Good speakers modulate their voices instead of shouting.
She modulated her tone the moment the children came in.
The drug works by modulating the immune response.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (modulate your voice), intransitive (the music modulates into a minor key)

entries.meaning: To add moisture to the skin, usually with a cream or a lotion. ---
examples: Dermatologists tell you to moisturize right after a shower.
She moisturized her face and went to bed.
Moisturizing twice a day fixed the cracks on my hands.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (moisturize your hands), intransitive (this cream moisturizes for hours)
entries.contrast: American spelling is moisturize; British writing uses moisturise.

entries.meaning: To touch or attack someone sexually, especially a child. ---
examples: State law requires anyone who tries to molest a child to be reported at once.
Prosecutors said the coach molested several players over a decade.
Two former campers testified that they had been molested there in the 1990s.
entries.contrast: An older sense meaning simply to bother or disturb survives in phrases like do not molest the wildlife; in ordinary modern American English molest is understood as sexual abuse.

entries.meaning: To calm someone's anger and make them feel less upset. ---
examples: An apology alone will not mollify the neighbors.
The refund mollified most of the customers.
The governor spent the week mollifying angry voters.
entries.contrast: Final -y becomes -ied: mollify → mollified, but mollifying keeps the y.

entries.meaning: To make money from something that did not earn money before, such as a website or an audience. ---
examples: Creators try to monetize their channels with ads and memberships.
The app monetized its user base by adding a subscription tier.
The blog has never been monetized at all.
entries.contrast: American spelling is monetize; British writing uses monetise.

entries.meaning: To take complete control of something so that no one else gets a share of it. ---
examples: Two firms monopolize the market for these chips.
He monopolized the conversation for the entire evening.
The court found that the company had illegally monopolized search advertising.

entries.meaning: To make the long, low sound that a cow makes. ---
examples: Cows moo when they want to be milked.
A calf mooed somewhere behind the barn.
The herd kept us awake, mooing half the night.

entries.meaning: To get money, food, or favors from other people instead of paying or working for them. ---
examples: He will mooch a ride home if you let him.
She mooched twenty dollars off her brother.
I am tired of him mooching meals from us.
entries.русский: клянчить, попрошайничать; жить за чужой счёт
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (he mooched a ride home), intransitive (she has been mooching all summer)
entries.contrast: Informal, and usually followed by off or from someone.

entries.meaning: To work a second job, usually in the evening, in addition to a full-time one. ---
examples: Plenty of teachers moonlight as tutors.
He moonlighted as a bartender while finishing law school.
She has been moonlighting for a rival firm.
entries.contrast: The past is regular, moonlighted, never moonlit; moonlit is only an adjective, as in a moonlit beach.

entries.meaning: To tie up a boat to the shore or to an anchor so that it stays in place. ---
examples: Fishermen moor their boats behind the breakwater.
We moored for the night in a quiet cove.
The ferry was moored at the far end of the pier.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (they moored the yacht), intransitive (we moored outside the harbor)

entries.meaning: To be quiet and miserable, showing that you feel sorry for yourself. ---
examples: Do not mope — call her and apologize.
He moped for a week after the team lost.
She spent the whole afternoon moping in her room.
entries.contrast: The past moped (MOHPT) is spelled like the noun moped (MOH-ped), the small motorbike, but sounds nothing like it.

entries.meaning: To talk or write about right and wrong in a way that sounds superior. ---
examples: Columnists love to moralize about other people's habits.
He moralized for ten minutes before handing back the tests.
The film tells the story without moralizing.

entries.meaning: To change gradually into something different, or to change one image into another. ---
examples: Small startups often morph into something their founders never planned.
The argument morphed into a full-blown fight.
The clip shows a caterpillar morphing into a butterfly.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the software morphs one face into another), intransitive (the protest morphed into a riot)

entries.meaning: To make someone feel deeply embarrassed or ashamed. ---
examples: Nothing mortifies a teenager like a parent at the school dance.
It mortified him to be corrected in front of the class.
I was mortified when I realized the microphone was still on.
entries.русский: смущать, вгонять в краску; сильно пристыдить

entries.meaning: To tell someone something with a movement of your hand or head instead of with words. ---
examples: Just motion to the waiter if you need anything.
The guard motioned us through the gate.
She stood there motioning frantically at the clock.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (she motioned him inside), intransitive (he motioned toward the door)

entries.meaning: To form words with your lips without making a sound, or to say words you do not really mean. ---
examples: Singers often mouth the words while a recording plays.
She mouthed "thank you" at me across the room.
Politicians keep mouthing the same promises every election.
entries.contrast: The noun mouth ends in the voiceless /θ/; the verb ends in the voiced /ð/, and its -s form is mouths /maʊðz/.

entries.meaning: To mix things up or confuse them so that they are no longer clear. ---
examples: Too many charts only muddle the argument.
He muddled the dates and missed the appointment.
By then my notes were hopelessly muddled.

entries.meaning: To make something dirty with mud, or to make a question less clear. ---
examples: Heavy rain will muddy the trail before morning.
The new evidence muddied the case.
Both sides are muddying the waters on purpose.
entries.contrast: Final -y gives muddies and muddied, but the -ing form keeps it: muddying.

entries.meaning: To think about something carefully for some time before deciding. ---
examples: The board will mull the offer for another week.
She mulled the question and said nothing.
He is still mulling whether to run again.
entries.contrast: Often used with over: she mulled the idea over for days.

entries.meaning: To do several things at the same time. ---
examples: Some people can genuinely multitask; most only think they can.
She multitasked through the whole call, answering email as she talked.
Multitasking behind the wheel is how accidents happen.
entries.русский: делать несколько дел одновременно, совмещать задачи

entries.meaning: To preserve a dead body by drying it and wrapping it, as the ancient Egyptians did. ---
examples: Egyptian priests would mummify a pharaoh over seventy days.
The dry desert air mummified the bodies naturally.
Dozens of mummified cats were found in the tomb.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (priests mummified the body), intransitive (the remains mummified in the dry air)

entries.meaning: To think about something quietly, or to say something in a slow, thoughtful way. ---
examples: Old letters make you muse on how much has changed.
"We could just sell the house," she mused.
He sat by the window, musing about the year ahead.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive ("Maybe she was right," he mused), intransitive (she mused about her childhood)

entries.meaning: To grow or increase very quickly and without control. ---
examples: Costs mushroom as soon as the lawyers get involved.
The town mushroomed after the factory opened.
Complaints have been mushrooming since the update.

entries.meaning: To gather people, votes, or feelings such as courage together. ---
examples: He could barely muster the courage to ask.
The bill mustered only forty votes.
Volunteers were mustering in the parking lot before sunrise.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (muster support), intransitive (the troops mustered at dawn)

entries.meaning: To change in form or structure, especially when a gene or a virus changes. ---
examples: Flu viruses mutate from one season to the next.
The strain mutated twice in a single winter.
Cells that have mutated may start growing out of control.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (radiation mutates cells), intransitive (the virus mutates quickly)

entries.meaning: To damage something severely, especially by cutting off or destroying part of a body. ---
examples: Vandals mutilate the statues in the park almost every summer.
The accident mutilated his left hand.
Several library books had been mutilated, with whole pages torn out.

entries.meaning: To refuse to obey the officers in charge, especially on a ship or in an army. ---
examples: Crews mutiny only when conditions become unbearable.
The sailors mutinied off the coast of Chile.
Two other ships had mutinied the week before.
entries.contrast: Final -y gives mutinies and mutinied, but the -ing form keeps it: mutinying.

entries.meaning: To put a guard over an animal's mouth, or to stop a person or the press from speaking freely. ---
examples: The city requires owners to muzzle certain breeds in public.
The new law effectively muzzled the opposition press.
The dog was muzzled and kept on a short leash.
entries.русский: надевать намордник; затыкать рот, заставлять молчать

entries.meaning: To confuse someone completely, because a thing cannot be explained. ---
examples: The rules of cricket mystify most Americans.
The disappearance mystified investigators for decades.
I was mystified by the extra charge on my statement.
entries.русский: озадачивать, ставить в тупик; сбить с толку

entries.meaning: To tell the story of a person or an event in a way that makes them seem grander and more heroic than they were. ---
examples: Sportswriters mythologize every quarterback who retires.
Hollywood mythologized the Old West for fifty years.
The founder has been thoroughly mythologized inside the company.

entries.meaning: To catch or grab someone or something quickly, often a criminal or a bargain. ---
examples: Police usually nab the driver within a mile.
She nabbed the last two tickets.
He was nabbed at the airport with the paintings in his bag.
entries.contrast: Informal. A single final consonant after a short vowel doubles: nab → nabbed, nabbing.

entries.meaning: To put a private company or industry under government ownership. ---
examples: Some countries nationalize their oil industry outright.
The government nationalized the banks during the crisis.
The railways were nationalized and then sold off again.
entries.contrast: American spelling is nationalize; British writing uses nationalise.

entries.meaning: To make someone a citizen of a country they were not born in. ---
examples: It can take years to naturalize as an American citizen.
The court naturalized two hundred applicants that morning.
Both of my grandparents were naturalized in 1954.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the court naturalized 200 applicants), intransitive (the plant has naturalized along the river)

entries.meaning: To make someone feel sick to their stomach, or deeply disgusted. ---
examples: Long car trips nauseate my younger brother.
The rocking of the boat nauseated half the passengers.
I was nauseated by the whole story.
entries.contrast: Nauseating describes the cause (a nauseating smell); nauseated describes the person who feels sick.

entries.meaning: To come closer to a place, a time, or a level. ---
examples: As we near the end of the year, budgets get tight.
The plane neared the runway and then pulled up again.
With the deadline nearing, the team worked through the night.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the ship neared the coast), intransitive (as the deadline neared)
entries.contrast: Near is also a preposition and an adjective, but as a verb it is completely regular: nears, neared, nearing.

entries.meaning: To make something necessary. ---
examples: Bad weather may necessitate a change of plan.
The injury necessitated two operations.
The move has necessitated hiring twenty more staff.

entries.meaning: To annoy someone with repeated teasing remarks or small criticisms. ---
examples: His brothers needle him about his accent.
The reporter needled the coach until he walked out.
She kept needling me about the money I owed her.

entries.meaning: To make the long, high sound that a horse makes. ---
examples: Horses neigh to each other across the field.
The mare neighed the moment she heard the bucket.
We could hear the horses neighing in the dark.
entries.contrast: Neigh sounds exactly like nay, the old word for no.

entries.meaning: To settle comfortably into a warm, soft, or sheltered place. ---
examples: Puppies nestle against each other to stay warm.
She nestled the sleeping baby into the car seat.
The village is nestled between two ridges.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (she nestled the baby against her shoulder), intransitive (the cat nestled into the blanket)
entries.contrast: The t is silent: NES-uhl, like castle and whistle.

entries.meaning: To operate on an animal so that it cannot produce young. ---
examples: Shelters neuter every animal before adoption.
We had the cat neutered at six months.
Neutering a dog usually stops it from roaming.
entries.contrast: In American English the first syllable is NOO-, not NYOO-.

entries.meaning: To stop something from having any effect, or to make a chemical or a threat harmless. ---
examples: A little baking soda will neutralize the acid.
The defense neutralized their best scorer.
The device was neutralized by the bomb squad.

entries.meaning: To make a small cut or notch in something, often by accident. ---
examples: Be careful not to nick the paint when you move the table.
He nicked his chin shaving.
The blade had nicked the bone.
entries.contrast: In British slang nick also means steal or arrest; American English uses it mainly for a small cut.

entries.meaning: To give a person or a thing an informal extra name. ---
examples: Teammates always nickname the new guy within a week.
The press nicknamed him the Iceman.
The tower is nicknamed the Cheese Grater.

entries.meaning: To bring something back to a normal state, or to make something unusual come to seem ordinary. ---
examples: The talks are meant to normalize relations between the two countries.
Prices normalized once the shortage ended.
Remote work has been normalized over the last five years.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (normalize relations), intransitive (trade normalized after the war)

entries.meaning: To fall steeply and suddenly, in value, in quality, or through the air. ---
examples: Ratings nosedive every time they change the schedule.
The stock nosedived after the recall.
Sales have nosedived since January.
entries.contrast: The past is nosedived, not nosedove, even though dive on its own can be dove.

entries.meaning: To heat food in a microwave, or, more seriously, to destroy something completely. ---
examples: Just nuke the leftovers for two minutes.
He nuked a burrito at midnight.
My draft got nuked when the app crashed.
entries.contrast: Informal in every sense; the microwave meaning is the one you hear most in American kitchens.

entries.meaning: To make something unclear or hard to understand, usually on purpose. ---
examples: Jargon can obfuscate a perfectly simple idea.
The report obfuscated the real cost of the project.
They are obfuscating instead of answering the question.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the memo obfuscated the numbers), intransitive (stop obfuscating and answer)

entries.meaning: To treat a person as an object rather than as a human being with feelings. ---
examples: Ads that objectify women still get past the reviewers.
Critics said the show objectified its contestants.
She felt objectified by the questions she was asked.

entries.meaning: To destroy something so completely that nothing of it is left. ---
examples: One storm can obliterate a whole season's crop.
The fire obliterated every record in the basement.
The village was obliterated in a single night.
entries.русский: уничтожать, стирать с лица земли; стереть

entries.meaning: To remove a difficulty or make something unnecessary. ---
examples: A short walk to the office would obviate the need for a second car.
The new software obviated hours of manual checking.
Signing online has obviated the trip to the bank.

entries.meaning: To block a passage or opening, or to shut something out of view. ---
examples: Fatty deposits can occlude an artery and cause a heart attack.
Thick clouds occluded the moon all night.
The surgeon found the vessel almost completely occluded.

entries.meaning: To happen, especially without being planned. ---
examples: Strong aftershocks occur for weeks after a big quake.
The crash occurred just after midnight.
Outages have been occurring almost every week.
entries.contrast: The r doubles before an ending: occur → occurred → occurring.

entries.meaning: To take a load off something, or to get rid of something unwanted by passing it to someone else. ---
examples: Crews offload the containers as soon as the ship docks.
The bank offloaded its riskiest loans last year.
He is offloading half his work onto the new hire.

entries.meaning: To move work or production to another country, usually to cut costs. ---
examples: Some firms offshore their customer support to save money.
The company offshored two hundred jobs to Mexico.
Manufacturing has been steadily offshored since the nineties.
entries.русский: выводить за рубеж, вывести (производство, рабочие места)
entries.contrast: As an adjective offshore means out at sea (offshore drilling); the verb is about moving jobs abroad.

entries.meaning: To stare at someone or something in an open, often rude or greedy way. ---
examples: Tourists ogle the sports cars in the showroom window.
He ogled the dessert cart for a full minute.
She left because a man at the bar kept ogling her.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (he ogled the car), intransitive (stop ogling)

entries.meaning: To officially approve something. ---
examples: The manager has to okay every refund over fifty dollars.
Her doctor okayed the trip.
We are still waiting for the budget to be okayed.
entries.русский: одобрять, одобрить; давать добро, дать добро
entries.contrast: Also written OK, whose past is OK'd; okayed is the safer spelling in writing.

entries.meaning: To leave something out, on purpose or by mistake. ---
examples: Omit the middle name if the form has no room for it.
The report omitted the cost of repairs.
Two witnesses were omitted from the list.
entries.contrast: The t doubles: omit → omitted → omitting.

entries.meaning: To state an opinion, often formally or a little self-importantly. ---
examples: Cable hosts opine about the economy for hours every night.
The judge opined that the contract was unenforceable.
He was still opining on tax policy when we left.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (he opined that the plan would fail), intransitive (columnists opine for a living)

entries.meaning: To choose one thing rather than another. ---
examples: Most students opt for the online version of the course.
She opted to take the train instead of flying.
More buyers are opting for hybrids this year.
entries.contrast: Opt takes for before a noun (opt for the blue one) and to before a verb (opt to wait).

entries.meaning: To make someone a priest or minister, or to order officially that something shall be so. ---
examples: The diocese will ordain six new priests in June.
She was ordained as a rabbi last spring.
The constitution ordains that only Congress may declare war.
entries.русский: посвящать в сан, посвятить; предписывать, предписать

entries.meaning: To leave a child without living parents, or to leave something without support or an owner. ---
examples: Wars orphan thousands of children every year.
He was orphaned at nine and raised by an aunt.
The company folded, orphaning the software its customers depended on.

entries.meaning: To swing back and forth, or to keep changing between two states or opinions. ---
examples: These fans oscillate so the air reaches the whole room.
The stock oscillated between forty and sixty dollars all year.
He kept oscillating between quitting and staying.

entries.meaning: To turn into bone, or to become rigid and unable to change. ---
examples: Cartilage begins to ossify in early childhood.
Decades of easy profits ossified the company's thinking.
The party has ossified into a set of slogans.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (routine ossified the department), intransitive (the cartilage ossifies)
entries.contrast: The -y becomes -ie- in ossifies and ossified, but stays in ossifying.

entries.meaning: To force someone out of a position or place of power. ---
examples: Shareholders can oust a chief executive with a single vote.
Protesters ousted the president after three weeks in the streets.
She was ousted from the board in April.

entries.meaning: To do better than a rival and take its business, resources, or territory. ---
examples: Small stores cannot outcompete a warehouse chain on price.
The invasive weed outcompeted every native plant in the field.
Cheap imports have outcompeted local producers for a decade.
entries.русский: побеждать в конкуренции, победить; обходить конкурентов, обойти

entries.meaning: To earn more money than someone else. ---
examples: Nurses with a master's degree often outearn their supervisors.
She outearned her husband from the day they married.
Graduates have consistently outearned classmates who left school early.

entries.meaning: To get around the side of an opponent, in battle or in an argument. ---
examples: Light cavalry could outflank a slower army.
The senator outflanked her critics by releasing the tapes herself.
The defense was outflanked in the first ten minutes.
entries.русский: обходить с фланга, обойти; переигрывать, переиграть

entries.meaning: To beat someone by being cleverer or craftier than they are. ---
examples: A good defense attorney can outfox the prosecution.
The raccoons outfoxed every lock we put on the trash cans.
He has outfoxed bigger rivals before.

entries.meaning: To have more firepower or greater strength than an opponent. ---
examples: Two destroyers can easily outgun a patrol boat.
The visitors outgunned us in the second half, thirty to seven.
Small farmers are outgunned by the lobbyists in Washington.
entries.русский: превосходить в огневой мощи, превзойти; подавлять численностью
entries.contrast: The n doubles: outgun → outgunned → outgunning.

entries.meaning: To gain an advantage over someone by moving or acting more skillfully. ---
examples: A smaller ship can often outmaneuver a battleship.
She outmaneuvered three rivals to win the contract.
The governor has been outmaneuvered at every turn.
entries.contrast: American outmaneuver; British writing has outmanoeuvre.

entries.meaning: To be clearly better or stronger than someone or something. ---
examples: No local team can outmatch them on defense.
Their budget outmatched ours ten to one.
He was badly outmatched in the final round.

entries.meaning: To make people extremely angry by doing something shocking or unfair. ---
examples: Cuts to school lunches outrage parents every time.
The verdict outraged the whole city.
Readers were outraged by the photograph.
entries.русский: возмущать, возмутить; приводить в ярость, привести в ярость

entries.meaning: To hold a higher position or rank than someone else. ---
examples: A sergeant outranks a corporal.
She outranked everyone else in the room.
He forgot that he was outranked by the woman he was shouting at.
entries.русский: быть выше по званию; превосходить по рангу, превзойти

entries.meaning: To defeat someone by being cleverer than they are. ---
examples: You cannot outsmart a machine that never gets tired.
The squirrels outsmarted our new bird feeder in a day.
He thought he was outsmarting the tax office.

entries.meaning: To become greater or faster than something else, or to leave a rival behind. ---
examples: Demand for chargers could outstrip supply by next winter.
Costs outstripped the budget within three months.
Prices have been outstripping wages for years.
entries.contrast: The p doubles: outstrip → outstripped → outstripping.

entries.meaning: To be more important or more valuable than something else. ---
examples: The benefits clearly outweigh the risks.
Convenience outweighed the price for most buyers.
The costs have long outweighed whatever the program achieved.

entries.meaning: To beat someone using cleverness rather than force. ---
examples: In the story a farmer's daughter outwits the king.
The thieves outwitted every alarm in the building.
He spends the whole movie outwitting the police.
entries.contrast: The t doubles: outwit → outwitted → outwitting.

entries.meaning: To act with exaggerated emotion, especially on stage or on camera. ---
examples: Young actors often overact in close-ups.
He overacted the death scene so badly that the audience laughed.
She is overacting, but the part calls for it.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (he overacted the death scene), intransitive (the whole cast overacts)

entries.meaning: To think about something in far more detail than it needs. ---
examples: Try not to overanalyze a two-line text message.
We overanalyzed the data and missed the obvious answer.
He has been overanalyzing that conversation for a week.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (don't overanalyze the text), intransitive (I tend to overanalyze)
entries.contrast: American overanalyze; British writing has overanalyse.

entries.meaning: To charge someone more than the correct amount. ---
examples: Some clinics overbill insurers for routine tests.
The contractor overbilled us by four thousand dollars.
Thousands of customers were overbilled for two years.
entries.русский: выставлять завышенный счёт, выставить завышенный счёт

entries.meaning: To sell more seats or rooms than actually exist. ---
examples: Airlines routinely overbook popular flights.
The hotel overbooked and put us in a motel by the highway.
Our flight was overbooked, so they offered us a voucher.
entries.русский: продавать больше мест, чем есть; перебронировать
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (airlines overbook flights), intransitive (the hotel overbooked again)

entries.meaning: To give someone or something more work or weight than it can handle. ---
examples: New rules should not overburden small businesses.
The storm overburdened the city's drains.
Teachers here are overburdened and underpaid.

entries.meaning: To promise more time, money, or effort than you can actually give. ---
examples: Do not overcommit in your first month on the job.
We overcommitted to three projects and finished none of them.
She is overcommitting herself again this semester.
entries.русский: брать на себя слишком много, взять на себя слишком много
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (don't overcommit your team), intransitive (I overcommitted again)
entries.contrast: The t doubles: overcommit → overcommitted → overcommitting.

entries.meaning: To go too far in fixing something and create the opposite problem. ---
examples: Do not overcorrect if the car starts to slide on ice.
He overcorrected on the shoulder and rolled the truck.
The bank, overcorrecting for last year's losses, stopped lending altogether.
entries.русский: чрезмерно исправлять, исправить; перестараться с поправкой
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (editors overcorrect student writing), intransitive (he overcorrected and spun out)

entries.meaning: To put too many people or things into a space. ---
examples: Budget cuts overcrowd every classroom in the district.
Tourists overcrowded the little harbor town all July.
The shelter is dangerously overcrowded.

entries.meaning: To take, or to give someone, a dangerously large amount of a drug. ---
examples: Teenagers who overdose on these pills often stop breathing.
He overdosed twice before he agreed to go to treatment.
She nearly died after overdosing on her mother's medication.
entries.русский: принимать слишком большую дозу, принять слишком большую дозу; передозировать
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (a nurse overdosed the patient), intransitive (he overdosed on painkillers)
entries.contrast: The noun is stressed on the first syllable, OH-vur-dohs; the verb on the last, oh-vur-DOHS.

entries.meaning: To wear clothes that are too formal or too warm for the occasion. ---
examples: It is better to overdress than to show up in shorts.
I overdressed for the interview and felt ridiculous.
The baby was overdressed for a seventy-degree day.
entries.русский: одеваться слишком нарядно, одеться слишком нарядно; кутать, закутать
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (don't overdress the baby), intransitive (I always overdress)

entries.meaning: To give something more importance than it deserves. ---
examples: Coaches sometimes overemphasize size and ignore speed.
The article overemphasized one bad quarter.
Test scores have been wildly overemphasized in this district.
entries.contrast: American overemphasize; British writing has overemphasise.

entries.meaning: To think something is bigger, better, or more likely than it really is. ---
examples: Do not overestimate how much a coat of paint can hide.
We badly overestimated the size of the crowd.
His influence has been consistently overestimated.
entries.contrast: The verb ends in a full vowel, oh-vur-ES-tuh-mayt; the noun ends in a schwa, oh-vur-ES-tuh-muht.

entries.meaning: To push yourself so hard physically that you do yourself harm. ---
examples: Patients recovering from surgery should not overexert themselves.
He overexerted himself shoveling snow and ended up in the emergency room.
She has been overexerting herself at the gym all month.

entries.meaning: To let something take in too much light, or to put someone in front of the public too much. ---
examples: Do not overexpose the shot, or the snow will come out pure white.
The studio overexposed its young star and audiences tired of her.
Half the roll was overexposed.

entries.meaning: To stretch yourself or your resources further than they can safely go. ---
examples: Do not overextend your credit to buy a bigger house.
The chain overextended itself and closed forty stores.
Supply lines were dangerously overextended.
entries.русский: перенапрягать силы, перенапрячь силы; брать на себя слишком много

entries.meaning: To take so many fish from an area that the population cannot recover. ---
examples: Trawlers overfish these waters every summer.
The Grand Banks were overfished until the cod collapsed.
Local fleets have been overfishing the bay for decades.
entries.русский: истощать запасы рыбы, истощить запасы рыбы; перелавливать

entries.meaning: To promote something far more than it deserves, so that people expect too much. ---
examples: Studios overhype almost every summer release.
The company overhyped the product and buyers were disappointed.
Critics say the threat has been badly overhyped.

entries.meaning: To have too much of something enjoyable, or to give someone far too much of what they want. ---
examples: It is easy to overindulge at a buffet.
We overindulged over the holidays and paid for it in January.
Grandparents are famous for overindulging their grandchildren.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (they overindulge their kids), intransitive (we overindulged at dinner)

entries.meaning: To put too much air into something, or to make something seem far bigger than it is. ---
examples: Do not overinflate the tires before a long drive.
The agency overinflated the number of visitors.
He has an overinflated sense of his own importance.

entries.meaning: To cover part of something else, or to happen partly at the same time as something else. ---
examples: Our shifts overlap by an hour every Friday.
The two studies overlapped almost completely.
The shingles are overlapping so that rain runs off.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the tiles overlap each other), intransitive (our shifts overlap)
entries.contrast: The verb stresses the last syllable, oh-vur-LAP; the noun stresses the first, OH-vur-lap. The p doubles: overlapped, overlapping.

entries.meaning: To put more weight, work, or data on something than it can carry. ---
examples: Do not overload the washing machine.
The storm overloaded the power grid.
Students are overloaded with assignments this term.
entries.contrast: Verb oh-vur-LOHD, noun OH-vur-lohd (an overload of information).

entries.meaning: To make something seem more important or more certain than it really is. ---
examples: Do not overplay the risk; the odds are still good.
The senator overplayed his hand and lost the vote.
Reporters have been overplaying one bad poll.

entries.meaning: To fill a place with more people or animals than it can support. ---
examples: Rabbits can overpopulate an island in a single season.
The deer overpopulated the park within a decade.
The lake is overpopulated with carp.

entries.meaning: To charge more for something than it is worth. ---
examples: Airport shops overprice everything.
They overpriced the house and it sat unsold for a year.
The wine list is wildly overpriced.
entries.русский: завышать цену, назначать слишком высокую цену

entries.meaning: To protect someone so much that you keep them from normal experience. ---
examples: Parents who overprotect their children leave them unprepared.
She admits she overprotected her youngest son.
He grew up feeling overprotected.

entries.meaning: To think someone or something is better or more important than it really is. ---
examples: Fans overrate any quarterback who wins early.
Most critics overrated the first album.
That restaurant is completely overrated.

entries.meaning: To try to do more than you can manage or have the right to do, and fail because of it. ---
examples: Startups often overreach in their second year.
The governor overreached and the courts struck the order down.
By overreaching, the union lost the gains it already had.
entries.русский: зарываться, брать на себя слишком много, переусердствовать
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive (the company overreached), transitive (he overreached himself)

entries.meaning: To react much more strongly than a situation deserves. ---
examples: Try not to overreact to one bad grade.
Management overreacted and fired the whole team.
He is overreacting, as usual.
entries.contrast: Followed by to: overreact to the news.

entries.meaning: To give a group more seats, places, or attention than its share of the population deserves. ---
examples: The Senate overrepresents small states.
Early surveys overrepresented homeowners.
Men are heavily overrepresented in the field.
entries.русский: представлять непропорционально широко; быть чрезмерно представленным

entries.meaning: To make something else seem less important or less noticed. ---
examples: One scandal can overshadow a decade of good work.
Her older brother's record overshadowed everything she did.
The news conference was overshadowed by the storm.

entries.meaning: To tell people more personal detail than they want to hear. ---
examples: Some coworkers overshare the minute they sit down.
He overshared about his divorce at the office party.
She apologized for oversharing online.
entries.русский: выбалтывать лишнее, рассказывать слишком много личного
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive (he overshares constantly), transitive (she overshared the details)

entries.meaning: To explain something so simply that what is left is misleading or wrong. ---
examples: Textbooks oversimplify the causes of the war.
The summary oversimplified a complicated ruling.
I am oversimplifying, but that is the basic idea.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the article oversimplifies the issue), intransitive (I am oversimplifying here)
entries.contrast: The -y becomes -ies and -ied: oversimplifies, oversimplified, but oversimplifying keeps the y.

entries.meaning: To describe something as larger, worse, or more certain than it really is. ---
examples: It is hard to overstate how much the city has changed.
The report overstated the savings by half.
The danger has been overstated from the beginning.

entries.meaning: To go beyond a limit of what is allowed or acceptable. ---
examples: Do not overstep your authority on this.
The agency overstepped its legal powers.
He knew he was overstepping the moment he said it.
entries.contrast: The p doubles: overstepped, overstepping. The old form overstept is not used in American English.

entries.meaning: To put more strain on someone or something than it can stand, or to tax people too heavily. ---
examples: Twelve-hour shifts overtax the nurses.
The climb overtaxed his knees.
Emergency rooms are overtaxed every flu season.

entries.meaning: To use something too much or too often, so that it wears out or loses its effect. ---
examples: Beginning writers overuse adverbs.
Doctors once overused antibiotics for ordinary colds.
The trail is badly overused in summer.
entries.contrast: The verb ends in a z-sound, oh-vur-YOOZ; the noun ends in an s-sound, OH-vur-yoos.

entries.meaning: To decide or state that something is worth more than it really is. ---
examples: Investors overvalue companies that grow fast early on.
The bank overvalued the property by two hundred thousand dollars.
The currency is overvalued against the dollar.

entries.meaning: To work too hard, or to make someone work too hard. ---
examples: Small clinics overwork their nurses.
She overworked all spring and got sick in May.
The crew looks overworked and underpaid.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the firm overworks its staff), intransitive (he overworks every spring)
entries.contrast: The past is overworked; overwrought is a different word, meaning very upset.

entries.meaning: To release an egg from the ovary. ---
examples: Most women ovulate about two weeks before a period.
She ovulated late that month, which threw off the calculation.
The app tracks the days she is ovulating.

entries.meaning: To add soft material to something to make it softer, thicker, or better protected. ---
examples: They pad the walls of the studio to deaden the sound.
She padded the box with newspaper before shipping it.
The jacket is padded at the shoulders.
entries.contrast: The d doubles: padded, padding. The same verb also means to add unnecessary extra, as in pad an expense report.

entries.meaning: To fasten or close something with a padlock. ---
examples: Crews padlock the gate at dusk.
The city padlocked the restaurant after two failed inspections.
Our bikes were padlocked to the rail.

entries.meaning: To call someone over a loudspeaker or by sending a message to a pager or phone. ---
examples: Page the on-call doctor right away.
They paged him twice in the terminal.
The nurse is paging the surgeon now.
entries.русский: вызывать по громкой связи, вызывать на пейджер

entries.meaning: To make someone feel hurt or unhappy. ---
examples: It pains me to see the old theater torn down.
Her silence pained him more than the argument had.
He was visibly pained by the question.
entries.contrast: As a verb pain is about feelings, and usually appears as it pains me to; for physical hurt Americans say hurt.

entries.meaning: To lose color in the face, or to seem small and unimportant beside something else. ---
examples: Other problems pale beside this one.
She paled when the police car pulled into the driveway.
Last year's delays have paled next to this year's.
entries.contrast: In the second sense it is nearly always pale in comparison with or pale beside something.

entries.meaning: To criticize a film, book, or show very harshly in a review. ---
examples: Critics pan almost every sequel.
Reviewers panned the movie as loud and lazy.
The show was panned by everyone except its fans.
entries.contrast: The n doubles: panned, panning. The same verb also means to swing a camera sideways (the camera pans left) and to wash gravel for gold (pan for gold).

entries.meaning: To say or do whatever will please a group, even when it is cheap or dishonest. ---
examples: Candidates pander to whoever turns out to vote.
The network pandered to its loudest viewers.
He is pandering, and everyone in the room knows it.
entries.contrast: Always with to: pander to voters.

entries.meaning: To beg strangers for money in a public place. ---
examples: People panhandle at that freeway exit all day.
He panhandled outside the station for a week.
A man was panhandling by the bus stop.

entries.meaning: To jump from an aircraft with a parachute, or to drop people or supplies by parachute. ---
examples: Smokejumpers parachute into fires no truck can reach.
The army parachuted food and blankets to the village.
She has parachuted from a plane twice.
entries.русский: прыгать с парашютом; сбрасывать на парашюте
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (they parachuted supplies in), intransitive (he parachuted into the valley)

entries.meaning: To be very similar to something else, or to run alongside it. ---
examples: Her career parallels his almost exactly.
The new road paralleled the river for ten miles.
Sales are paralleling last year's numbers.
entries.contrast: American English keeps one l: paralleled, paralleling; British writing doubles it.

entries.meaning: To boil food briefly so that it finishes cooking some other way. ---
examples: Parboil the potatoes for five minutes before roasting them.
She parboiled the ribs to shorten the time on the grill.
The carrots are parboiled, then tossed in oil and salt.

entries.meaning: To cut the skin or outer layer off something, or to cut something down to a smaller size. ---
examples: Pare the apples before you slice them.
The company pared its staff by a third.
Costs have been pared to the bone.
entries.русский: срезать, очищать от кожуры; урезать, сокращать
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like pair and pear, which are different words.

entries.meaning: To turn a small advantage into something much bigger. ---
examples: Athletes often parlay fame into a business.
She parlayed one viral video into a full-time job.
He is parlaying two terms on the city council into a run for governor.
entries.contrast: Not the same as parley, which means to hold talks with an opponent.

entries.meaning: To copy someone's style in an exaggerated way in order to make fun of it. ---
examples: Late-night shows parody whoever is in the news.
The sketch parodied the governor's accent.
His paintings have been parodied for decades.
entries.contrast: The -y becomes -ies and -ied: parodies, parodied, but parodying keeps the y.

entries.meaning: To repeat someone else's words without understanding or thinking about them. ---
examples: Kids parrot whatever they hear at home.
The anchor simply parroted the press release.
He was parroting lines from a movie.
entries.contrast: The t does not double, because the stress is on the first syllable: parroted, parroting.

entries.meaning: To divide a country, a room, or a disk into separate parts. ---
examples: Folding screens partition the hall for small events.
Britain partitioned India in 1947.
The drive has been partitioned into two volumes.

entries.meaning: To heat milk, juice, or another liquid enough to kill harmful bacteria. ---
examples: Dairies pasteurize milk before it is bottled.
They pasteurized the cider at a low temperature.
Most cheese sold here is made from pasteurized milk.
entries.contrast: American spelling is pasteurize; British writing uses pasteurise.

entries.meaning: To obtain an official right that stops others from making or selling your invention. ---
examples: Large firms patent thousands of small improvements a year.
He patented the design in 1974.
The process was patented by a lab in Ohio.

entries.meaning: To sell goods from place to place, or to spread ideas that others think worthless or false. ---
examples: Vendors peddle umbrellas the moment it rains.
He peddled insurance door to door for years.
The site has been peddling conspiracy theories for months.
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like pedal, which means to push the pedals of a bicycle.

entries.meaning: To urinate. ---
examples: The dog needs to pee before bed.
He peed in the bushes halfway up the trail.
The baby has been peeing through her diapers all week.
entries.contrast: Informal but completely ordinary in speech and with doctors; in formal or medical writing use urinate.

entries.meaning: To look quickly and secretly, especially through a small opening. ---
examples: Kids peep through the fence to watch practice.
She peeped around the corner to see who was there.
He was peeping through the blinds when the car pulled up.
entries.contrast: Peek is a quick innocent look; peep often suggests spying, as in Peeping Tom.

entries.meaning: To annoy someone in a small, nagging way. ---
examples: Little things peeve him more than big ones.
It peeved her that nobody said thank you.
He looked peeved when I mentioned the delay.

entries.meaning: To fix a price, rate, or number at a set level, usually tied to something else. ---
examples: Several countries peg their currency to the dollar.
The board pegged the raise at three percent.
Rents are pegged to the cost-of-living index.
entries.contrast: The g doubles: pegged, pegging. Informally, peg someone as means to size them up: I pegged him as a lawyer.

entries.meaning: To write something such as a letter, an article, or a song. ---
examples: Columnists pen the same editorial every spring.
She penned the letter the night before she left.
The song was penned by a teenager.
entries.contrast: The n doubles: penned, penning. Slightly literary; in ordinary speech people just say write.

entries.meaning: To get into or through something, especially when that is hard to do. ---
examples: Sunlight barely penetrates the forest floor.
The blade penetrated two inches of oak.
Foreign firms have penetrated the market faster than anyone expected.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the bullet penetrated the wall), intransitive (the cold penetrated to the bone)
