entries.meaning: To hit or cover something with many small things, or to fill speech or writing with a lot of something. ---
examples: Reporters pepper the mayor with questions after every meeting.
Hail peppered the roof for twenty minutes.
His essay is peppered with quotations.

entries.meaning: To make a hole or a line of small holes through something. ---
examples: Machines perforate the sheets so that they tear cleanly.
The ulcer perforated the wall of his stomach.
Stamps come perforated along the edges.

entries.meaning: To curl hair chemically so that the curls last for months. ---
examples: Salons still perm hair, though the style comes and goes.
She permed her hair for the wedding.
His mother had her hair permed every spring.

entries.meaning: To spread through every part of something. ---
examples: Damp permeates the whole basement in spring.
The smell of smoke permeated every room in the house.
A quiet optimism was permeating the campaign.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the smell permeated the house), intransitive (water permeates through the soil)

entries.meaning: To carry out something wrong, especially a crime or a hoax. ---
examples: Whoever perpetrates this kind of fraud rarely works alone.
They perpetrated a hoax that fooled three newspapers.
The attack was perpetrated by two men in a stolen car.
entries.contrast: Perpetrate is to commit a crime; perpetuate is to keep something going, as in perpetuate a myth.

entries.meaning: To be a perfect example of a quality, or to write about a thing as if it were a person. ---
examples: For many fans she personifies the whole team.
He personified everything the party wanted to show off.
Winter is often personified as an old man.
entries.contrast: The -y becomes -ies and -ied: personifies, personified, but personifying keeps the y.

entries.meaning: To be connected with or relevant to something. ---
examples: These rules pertain only to full-time staff.
The judge read every document that pertained to the sale.
Questions pertaining to salary go to human resources.
entries.contrast: Always with to. Formal: in speech people say relate to or be about.

entries.meaning: To worry or unsettle someone. ---
examples: Loud noises perturb the horses.
The news perturbed him more than he let on.
She seemed perturbed by the question.

entries.meaning: To read or look through something, either closely or, in looser modern use, casually. ---
examples: Take a minute to peruse the menu.
He perused the contract line by line.
She was perusing the shelves when I came in.
entries.contrast: Traditionally peruse means to read very carefully; many Americans now use it for casual browsing, so the context decides.

entries.meaning: To spread through every part of a place, a group, or a feeling. ---
examples: A smell of woodsmoke seems to pervade the whole cabin.
Anxiety pervaded the office in the week before the layoffs.
Corruption had pervaded every level of the agency.

entries.meaning: To twist something good into something corrupt or wrong. ---
examples: Lying to a grand jury can pervert the course of justice.
The scheme perverted a program meant to help small farmers.
His teaching was perverted by the people who came after him.
entries.contrast: The verb stresses the second syllable (pur-VURT); the noun pervert stresses the first (PUR-vurt).

entries.meaning: To make a formal written request to an authority. ---
examples: Residents plan to petition the city council for a stoplight.
She petitioned the court to reopen the case.
Thousands have petitioned for the law to be repealed.
entries.русский: ходатайствовать, подавать петицию; обращаться с прошением
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (petition the court), intransitive (petition for a new trial)

entries.meaning: To frighten someone so badly that they cannot move or think. ---
examples: Elevators still petrify my brother.
The fire alarm petrified the whole kindergarten class.
She stood petrified at the top of the ladder.
entries.русский: приводить в ужас, парализовать страхом; окаменевать
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (heights petrify him), intransitive (buried wood slowly petrifies)
entries.contrast: Consonant + -y: petrifies, petrified, but petrifying.

entries.meaning: To have casual affairs while married or in a serious relationship. ---
examples: Men who philander rarely keep it quiet for long.
He went on television to deny that he had ever philandered.
The paper ran three pages on the senator philandering during state trips.

entries.meaning: To talk or write at length about large general questions. ---
examples: We could philosophize about it all night and still not agree.
He philosophized about fate while we waited for the tow truck.
They were still philosophizing over cold coffee at two in the morning.
entries.contrast: American spelling uses -ize; British writing has philosophise.

entries.meaning: To trick people into giving up passwords or bank details with fake messages. ---
examples: Criminals phish for bank logins with fake delivery texts.
Two employees were phished on the same morning.
Somebody is phishing our customers using our own logo.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (they phished four employees), intransitive (scammers phish for passwords)
entries.contrast: Spelled with ph-, but pronounced exactly like fish.

entries.meaning: To jump into someone else's photograph as a joke. ---
examples: My brother tries to photobomb every family picture.
A seagull photobombed our wedding shot.
We got photobombed by a guy in a dinosaur costume.
entries.русский: влезать в чужой кадр, портить фотографию

entries.meaning: To edit a photograph digitally, especially to change how something looks. ---
examples: Please don't photoshop my face; leave the picture alone.
Someone photoshopped a shark into the flood photo.
The magazine admitted that the cover had been photoshopped.
entries.contrast: Double the p: photoshopped, photoshopping.

entries.meaning: To steal from someone's pocket or bag, usually in a crowd. ---
examples: Thieves pickpocket tourists on the cathedral steps every summer.
Someone pickpocketed her at the street fair.
He was pickpocketed on a crowded train in Rome.
entries.contrast: Stress is on the first syllable, so the t stays single: pickpocketed, pickpocketing.

entries.meaning: To eat a meal outdoors, on the grass or at a park table. ---
examples: Let's picnic by the river if it stays dry.
We picnicked under the big oak behind the museum.
Families were picnicking all along the lakeshore.
entries.contrast: Add a k before the ending: picnicked, picnicking — like panic and traffic.

entries.meaning: To label a person or thing narrowly, ignoring everything else about them. ---
examples: Critics love to pigeonhole young writers.
One early role pigeonholed her for a decade.
He hates being pigeonholed as a country singer.
entries.русский: навешивать ярлык, загонять в узкие рамки

entries.meaning: To make use of something that already exists in order to carry or support something else. ---
examples: Small clinics piggyback on the hospital's supply contract.
The startup piggybacked its launch on a big trade show.
They are piggybacking new fiber onto the old power poles.
entries.русский: пристраиваться к чему-либо, использовать как основу
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (piggyback a second bill onto the budget), intransitive (the app piggybacks on your phone's GPS)

entries.meaning: To steal small things, usually a little at a time. ---
examples: Kids pilfer candy the second you turn your back.
He pilfered a handful of change from the tip jar.
Someone has been pilfering pens from the supply closet.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (pilfer supplies), intransitive (an employee who pilfers)

entries.meaning: To rob a place violently, especially during a war. ---
examples: Raiders would pillage the coastal towns every spring.
The city was pillaged twice in the same century.
Soldiers spent three days pillaging the countryside.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (pillage a village), intransitive (the troops pillaged for days)

entries.meaning: To attack someone publicly and make them look ridiculous. ---
examples: Talk shows will pillory any candidate who says that out loud.
The press pilloried him for weeks over one bad quote.
She was pilloried online before the facts came out.
entries.русский: публично травить, выставлять на всеобщее осмеяние
entries.contrast: Consonant + -y: pillories, pilloried, but pillorying.

entries.meaning: To try a program or product out on a small scale before launching it fully. ---
examples: The district will pilot the new reading curriculum in four schools.
They piloted the app with two hundred users last fall.
A four-day week is being piloted at three of the company's plants.
entries.contrast: Stress on the first syllable, so the t stays single: piloted, piloting.

entries.meaning: To feel a deep, sad longing for someone or something you have lost. ---
examples: Don't pine for a city that has already forgotten you.
He pined for his old neighborhood for years after the move.
The dog spent a month pining by the front door.
entries.contrast: Normally takes for: you pine for someone.

entries.meaning: To find or describe something exactly. ---
examples: Engineers still can't pinpoint what caused the outage.
The survey pinpointed the leak within three feet.
Doctors have pinpointed the gene behind the disorder.

entries.meaning: To stir up someone's interest or curiosity. ---
examples: A good opening line should pique the reader's curiosity.
The headline piqued my interest enough to click.
The rumor has piqued the interest of two rival firms.
entries.contrast: Pronounced like peak. Drop the e before endings: piqued, piquing.

entries.meaning: To copy and distribute a film, song, book, or program illegally. ---
examples: Students still pirate expensive textbooks.
Someone pirated the movie before it reached theaters.
The album was being pirated within hours of release.
entries.contrast: Stress on the first syllable, so the t stays single: pirated, pirating.

entries.meaning: To spin all the way around on one foot, as a dancer does. ---
examples: She can pirouette four times without wobbling.
The skater pirouetted at center ice.
A dancer was pirouetting under a single spotlight.
entries.русский: делать пируэт, кружиться на одной ноге
entries.contrast: Double the t: pirouetted, pirouetting.

entries.meaning: To set one person or group against another in a contest. ---
examples: The playoff will pit last year's champion against a rookie team.
The water bill pitted farmers against ranchers.
Two old friends are being pitted against each other for the job.
entries.contrast: Double the t: pitted, pitting. Usually pit someone against someone.

entries.meaning: To blur part of an image into visible squares so that it cannot be identified. ---
examples: News editors pixelate the faces of minors.
The station pixelated the license plate before airing the clip.
His face was pixelated in every frame.
entries.contrast: American spelling has one l: pixelate, not pixellate.

entries.meaning: To cause trouble to someone or something again and again. ---
examples: Delays continue to plague the project.
Injuries plagued him all season.
The building has been plagued by leaks since it opened.
entries.contrast: The u stays in every form: plagued, plaguing.

entries.meaning: To shave a thin layer off wood so that it becomes smooth or flat. ---
examples: You'll have to plane the bottom of the door so it clears the rug.
He planed the boards until they sat flush.
She spent the afternoon planing the tabletop by hand.

entries.meaning: To arrange food on a plate for serving. ---
examples: Plate the fish while the sauce is still hot.
He plated forty entrées in twenty minutes.
The desserts were plated with a sprig of mint.
entries.русский: выкладывать на тарелку, оформлять блюдо; покрывать металлом
entries.contrast: A second sense is to coat with metal: a gold-plated watch.

entries.meaning: To stop rising and stay at the same level. ---
examples: Sales usually plateau in the third year.
Her weight loss plateaued after four months.
Case numbers have been plateauing since April.
entries.contrast: The French spelling is kept before endings: plateaued, plateauing.

entries.meaning: To walk or work slowly and heavily, without energy. ---
examples: The horses plod up the hill with the wagon.
We plodded through the last two miles in the rain.
He is still plodding through a four-hundred-page report.
entries.contrast: Double the d: plodded, plodding.

entries.meaning: To drop or sit down heavily, usually with a soft sound. ---
examples: Just plop the groceries on the table.
She plopped down on the couch without taking off her coat.
Rain was plopping into the bucket under the leak.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (plop the bag on the counter), intransitive (a frog plopped into the pond)
entries.contrast: Double the p: plopped, plopping.

entries.meaning: To explore or measure something all the way to its deepest point. ---
examples: Historians are still trying to plumb the meaning of the letters.
The documentary plumbed the family's whole history.
He has plumbed every corner of the archive.
entries.contrast: The b is silent: plumb sounds exactly like plum.

entries.meaning: To take goods from a place by force, or to use up something valuable. ---
examples: Treasure hunters plunder wrecks all along this coast.
The invaders plundered the monastery.
The pension fund had been plundered long before the audit.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (plunder a tomb), intransitive (the army plundered for days)

entries.meaning: To put a word into its plural form. ---
examples: Most English nouns pluralize with a simple s.
He pluralized the noun wrongly and wrote childs instead of children.
Nouns ending in a consonant plus y are pluralized with -ies.
entries.русский: ставить во множественное число, образовывать множественное число
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (pluralize a noun), intransitive (this noun pluralizes irregularly)
entries.contrast: American spelling uses -ize; British writing has pluralise.

entries.meaning: To work steadily at a trade, or to keep supplying someone with something. ---
examples: Street vendors ply their trade outside the stadium.
They plied us with coffee until midnight.
Ferries have plied this route since 1890.
entries.contrast: Consonant + -y: plies, plied, but plying.

entries.meaning: To aim your finger or an object at something to show where it is. ---
examples: Don't point at people; it's rude.
She pointed the flashlight into the crawlspace.
He was pointing toward the exit when the lights went out.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (point the flashlight at the door), intransitive (don't point)

entries.meaning: To hold something balanced and ready, or to be set to do something at any moment. ---
examples: She poised the needle over the record.
The team is poised to win its first title in forty years.
Hawks hunt by poising above a field and then dropping.
entries.русский: быть наготове, замереть в готовности; удерживать в равновесии
entries.contrast: Usually met in the passive: poised to launch, poised for a comeback. Not the same as pose, which is to hold a position for a picture.

entries.meaning: To split people into two groups with completely opposite opinions. ---
examples: Few issues polarize voters the way this one does.
The ruling polarized the country overnight.
Debate over the pipeline has polarized the whole county.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the ruling polarized the country), intransitive (opinion polarized quickly)

entries.meaning: To turn something into a political issue. ---
examples: Both sides politicize every hurricane response.
The hearing politicized what had been a technical question.
Science funding has been thoroughly politicized.
entries.contrast: American spelling uses -ize; British writing has politicise.

entries.meaning: To speak about something pompously, as if you were the final authority. ---
examples: He'll pontificate about wine for an hour if you let him.
She pontificated on parenting to a room full of parents.
They were still pontificating when the meeting ran out of time.

entries.meaning: To burst, or to make something burst, with a short sharp sound. ---
examples: One more nail and that tire will pop.
The cork popped and hit the ceiling.
The kids are popping bubble wrap in the hallway.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (pop a balloon), intransitive (the cork popped)
entries.contrast: Double the p: popped, popping.

entries.meaning: To make something known and liked by ordinary people. ---
examples: A single TV show can popularize a forgotten dish.
Carl Sagan popularized astronomy for a whole generation.
The style was popularized by two films in the same year.

entries.meaning: To fill a place with people or animals, or to fill a form or list with data. ---
examples: Otters again populate the lower river.
Settlers populated the valley in less than a decade.
The dropdown is populated from the customer database.

entries.meaning: To move a program so that it runs on a different system or device. ---
examples: They plan to port the game to consoles next spring.
We ported the whole app to Android in six weeks.
The tool has been ported to three operating systems.

entries.meaning: To be a sign that something, usually bad, is going to happen. ---
examples: Falling orders often portend layoffs.
The quiet market portended a rough winter.
Analysts read the drop as portending a longer slump.

entries.meaning: To divide something into shares or servings. ---
examples: Portion the stew into containers before it cools.
She portioned the rice into six bowls.
The meat comes already portioned and frozen.

entries.meaning: To put an idea forward as a basis for argument. ---
examples: Some economists posit a link between the two trends.
The paper posited that memory works like a search engine.
He is positing a much older date for the ruins.
entries.contrast: Stress on the first syllable, so the t stays single: posited, positing.

entries.meaning: To put a later date on a document than the day you write it, or to come later in time than something else. ---
examples: Don't postdate the check; the landlord won't take it.
She postdated the invoice to the first of the month.
Some employers get around the rule by postdating the paperwork.
entries.русский: датировать более поздним числом; быть позднее по времени
entries.contrast: The opposite of backdate: a postdated check is dated in the future.

entries.meaning: To stamp mail with the date and place it was sent. ---
examples: Entries must be postmarked by March 1.
The clerk postmarked every envelope by hand.
Our office postmarks outgoing mail twice a day.

entries.meaning: To assume something is true as a starting point for reasoning. ---
examples: The theory has to postulate a force nobody has measured.
Einstein postulated that the speed of light never changes.
He builds the whole argument by postulating a perfectly rational buyer.
entries.contrast: The verb ends -ayt (PAHS-chuh-layt); the noun postulate ends with a weak -uht.

entries.meaning: To behave in a way meant to impress people rather than to achieve anything. ---
examples: Both parties posture for the cameras before every vote.
He postured about being tough on crime and then did nothing.
They were only posturing; nobody intended to walk out.
entries.русский: рисоваться, играть на публику, принимать позу

entries.meaning: To push out your lips and look sulky because you are annoyed. ---
examples: He'll pout for an hour if he loses.
She pouted when we said no to a second movie.
The toddler was pouting in the corner of the sofa.

entries.meaning: To cover something with a fine dry dust such as sugar, flour, or makeup. ---
examples: Powder the pan with flour before you pour the batter.
She powdered her nose in the hallway mirror.
The doughnuts came out powdered with cinnamon sugar.

entries.meaning: To move with high, springy steps, often in a showy way. ---
examples: The colts prance along the fence line every morning.
He pranced onto the stage in a gold jacket.
She came prancing down the hall in her new boots.

entries.meaning: To talk on and on about unimportant things. ---
examples: Let him prattle; he'll wear himself out.
The host prattled through the whole award ceremony.
Two kids were prattling away in the back seat.

entries.meaning: To come or go before something else in time or order. ---
examples: A short film will precede the feature.
Two smaller quakes preceded the big one.
The chapter is preceded by a long author's note.
entries.contrast: Spelled -cede, unlike proceed (to go ahead) and supersede.

entries.meaning: To make something impossible or to rule it out in advance. ---
examples: A guilty plea does not preclude an appeal.
The injury precluded him from playing in the final.
Those terms have precluded several serious bidders.

entries.meaning: To exist or happen earlier than something else. ---
examples: These stone walls predate the town by two hundred years.
The rule predated the internet and made no sense anymore.
Anything predating 1950 goes straight to the archive.

entries.meaning: To fix someone's fate in advance, as if by fate or a higher power. ---
examples: Nothing in his childhood seemed to predestine him for the pulpit.
The novel argues that grief predestined every choice she made.
He talked as if he had been predestined to fail.

entries.meaning: To decide or fix something in advance. ---
examples: A zip code should not predetermine a child's future.
The budget predetermined which programs would survive.
Each sale price was predetermined by the auction house.

entries.meaning: To base something on a particular fact or assumption. ---
examples: Don't predicate the whole plan on one grant.
They predicated their forecast on steady fuel prices.
The argument is predicated on a single small study.
entries.contrast: The verb ends -ayt; the grammar term predicate ends with a weak -uht. Normally predicate something on something.

entries.meaning: To make someone more likely to have a condition, an opinion, or a reaction. ---
examples: Certain genes predispose people to high blood pressure.
A rough first week predisposed her to dislike the job.
Smokers are predisposed to this kind of infection.
entries.contrast: Predispose someone to something.

entries.meaning: To be the largest or strongest element in something. ---
examples: Pines predominate on the north slope.
Small farms predominated in the region until the 1970s.
With oak and maple predominating, the woods turn red in October.
entries.contrast: The adjective is predominant; the verb ends -ate.

entries.meaning: To smooth one's feathers, or to fuss over one's looks and enjoy the attention. ---
examples: Gulls preen on the pilings all afternoon.
He preened while the photographers shouted his name.
She was preening over that review for a week.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the swan preened its feathers), intransitive (he preened in front of the mirror)

entries.meaning: To exist before something else. ---
examples: These trails preexist every map we have of the park.
The crack preexisted the earthquake, the inspector said.
Insurers once refused to cover preexisting conditions.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the forest preexists the town), intransitive (the damage preexisted)
entries.contrast: American dictionaries write it solid — preexisting — though the press often hyphenates pre-existing.

entries.meaning: To build the parts of something in a factory so it can be assembled quickly on site. ---
examples: The company prefabricates whole bathrooms in Ohio.
They prefabricated the roof trusses before the concrete was poured.
Half the school is made of prefabricated panels.

entries.meaning: To say or write something as an introduction to what comes next. ---
examples: She likes to preface bad news with a joke.
He prefaced his answer with a long apology.
The report is prefaced by a letter from the governor.
entries.contrast: Stress stays on the first syllable — PREF-uhs, not pre-FAYS. Preface something with something.

entries.meaning: To put something at the front of a word, a name, or a list. ---
examples: You can prefix almost any verb with re-.
The editor prefixed each chapter with a short quotation.
Every file name is prefixed with the date.
entries.contrast: The verb stresses the second syllable (pree-FIKS); the noun prefix stresses the first (PREE-fiks).

entries.meaning: To form an opinion about something before you know the facts. ---
examples: Try not to prejudge the case from a headline.
The panel prejudged her application the moment they saw the school.
Nobody wants to be prejudged by an algorithm.

entries.meaning: To make someone biased, or to damage someone's chances or legal position. ---
examples: Pretrial publicity can prejudice a jury.
The leaked memo prejudiced the whole negotiation.
The judge ruled that the delay had not prejudiced the defense.

entries.meaning: To plan an act, usually a crime, in advance. ---
examples: The state must show that he premeditated the killing.
Nothing suggests the attack was premeditated.
Prosecutors argued that she spent weeks premeditating the theft.

entries.meaning: To base an argument or a plan on a stated assumption. ---
examples: The authors premise their whole case on one survey.
He premised the offer on the deal closing by June.
The show is premised on a simple what-if question.
entries.contrast: Almost always premised on something.

entries.meaning: To fill someone's mind so completely that they can think of little else. ---
examples: Money worries preoccupy half the staff.
The missing dog preoccupied the children all week.
He seemed preoccupied with something he wouldn't name.
entries.contrast: Consonant + -y: preoccupies, preoccupied, but preoccupying.

entries.meaning: To order something before it is available to buy. ---
examples: You can preorder the console starting Friday.
She preordered the book six months early.
Thousands of copies had been preordered by launch day.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (preorder the console), intransitive (preorder now and save)

entries.meaning: To record something in advance so that it can be played later. ---
examples: They prerecord the holiday episodes in August.
The station prerecorded his interview on Tuesday.
You will hear a prerecorded message about the outage.

entries.meaning: To sign up for something in advance. ---
examples: Preregister online and skip the line at the door.
Two hundred people preregistered for the clinic.
Students who have preregistered pick their rooms first.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (preregister your child), intransitive (preregister online by Friday)

entries.meaning: To be a sign or warning of something that is about to happen. ---
examples: A run on the bank can presage a much wider panic.
The resignations presaged a complete shake-up.
Nobody read the memo as presaging a merger.
entries.contrast: Usually PRES-ij for both the noun and the verb, though pri-SAYJ is also heard for the verb.

entries.meaning: To be formally in charge of a meeting, ceremony, or court. ---
examples: Judge Alvarez will preside at the hearing on Monday.
She presided over the committee for eight years.
The bishop has presided at every ordination since 2015.
entries.contrast: Always takes over or at: preside over a meeting, never preside a meeting.

entries.meaning: To keep the air or fluid inside something at a controlled pressure. ---
examples: Engineers pressurize the cabin so passengers can breathe at altitude.
The crew pressurized the airlock before opening the inner door.
The tank is pressurized to about thirty pounds per square inch.
entries.contrast: In American English you pressure a person (they pressured him to resign) but pressurize a cabin or a tank.

entries.meaning: To take something as true from the start, as the basis of an argument or plan. ---
examples: The whole plan presupposes that the funding is approved.
His question presupposed that I had already read the report.
Fair play cannot simply be presupposed; it has to be enforced.

entries.meaning: To avoid telling the plain truth by speaking evasively. ---
examples: Answer the question and do not prevaricate.
The witness prevaricated for twenty minutes.
He was still prevaricating when the hearing ended.

entries.meaning: To make a small hole in something with a sharp point. ---
examples: Prick the potatoes with a fork before baking them.
She pricked her finger on a thorn.
The nurse has already pricked his thumb for the blood test.

entries.meaning: To cause or feel a light stinging, tingling sensation on the skin. ---
examples: Cheap wool sweaters prickle if you wear them next to the skin.
The cold air prickled her cheeks.
His scalp was prickling with sweat.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the wool prickled my neck), intransitive (my skin prickled)

entries.meaning: To be proud of a quality or achievement of your own. ---
examples: They pride themselves on answering every email within a day.
She prided herself on never missing a deadline.
He has always prided himself on his memory for names.
entries.contrast: Only reflexive, and always with on: pride yourself on something, never I pride my work.

entries.meaning: To prepare something or someone in advance so that it is ready to work or respond. ---
examples: Prime the wall before you paint it.
The lawyer primed her client for the cross-examination.
The pump has to be primed with water before it will draw.

entries.meaning: To value something very highly. ---
examples: Collectors prize early editions of the book.
She prized her grandmother's ring above everything else she owned.
Quiet competence is prized at this company.
entries.contrast: British writing also uses prise for forcing something open; American English writes pry for that.

entries.meaning: To announce something publicly and with emphasis. ---
examples: The mayor will proclaim Saturday a day of remembrance.
He proclaimed himself the winner before the votes were counted.
Independence was proclaimed on the radio that morning.

entries.meaning: To produce young. ---
examples: Pandas rarely procreate in captivity.
The pair procreated twice in five years.
The colony is procreating faster than the biologists expected.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (procreate offspring), intransitive (pandas rarely procreate in captivity)

entries.meaning: To obtain something, especially with effort or through official channels. ---
examples: The agency procures uniforms for the whole department.
He procured a visa in less than a week.
Most of the equipment was procured from local suppliers.

entries.meaning: To claim something openly, often when the claim may not be sincere. ---
examples: Candidates profess concern about housing every election year.
She professed to know nothing about the transfer.
He has professed his innocence from the first day.

entries.meaning: To offer something formally, holding it out for the other side to accept. ---
examples: Witnesses may proffer documents to the court.
She proffered her hand, and he shook it.
No explanation has been proffered by the company.
entries.contrast: The stress is on the first syllable, so the r does not double: proffered, proffering.

entries.meaning: To make an unfair profit out of a shortage or a crisis. ---
examples: Some sellers profiteer whenever there is a shortage.
Contractors profiteered during the reconstruction.
Companies accused of profiteering were called before Congress.

entries.meaning: To increase quickly in number and spread widely. ---
examples: Delivery apps proliferate in every big city.
Rumors proliferated in the hours after the announcement.
Cheap drones have proliferated over the past decade.
entries.русский: быстро распространяться, расти в числе; размножаться

entries.meaning: To put a law or rule into effect by announcing it officially. ---
examples: Agencies promulgate rules only after a public comment period.
The council promulgated the new building code in March.
The standards were promulgated without much debate.

entries.meaning: To support something by leaning it against a surface or placing a support under it. ---
examples: Prop the door open with that brick.
He propped his bike against the fence.
Her chin was propped on both hands.
entries.contrast: Short vowel, so the p doubles: propped, propping.

entries.meaning: To drive something forward. ---
examples: Two small motors propel the boat.
The scandal propelled her into national politics.
The craft is propelled by the solar wind.
entries.contrast: Stress falls on the last syllable, so the l doubles: propelled, propelling.

entries.meaning: To say what will happen in the future, especially as an inspired prediction. ---
examples: Analysts prophesy a hard winter for retailers.
He prophesied the collapse two years before it came.
Everything she had prophesied came true.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (he prophesied a crash), intransitive (she prophesies for a living)
entries.contrast: The verb prophesy ends in -sy and rhymes with sigh; the noun prophecy ends in -cy and rhymes with see.

entries.meaning: To divide or charge an amount in proportion to the time or share actually used. ---
examples: We prorate the rent if you move in mid-month.
The airline prorated the refund for the unused leg.
Your first bill will be prorated from the day of installation.

entries.meaning: To forbid something officially. ---
examples: Federal law proscribes discrimination in hiring.
The regime proscribed every opposition party.
Several additives are proscribed in baby food.
entries.contrast: Proscribe means forbid; prescribe means order or recommend. A doctor prescribes a drug, a law proscribes it.

entries.meaning: To try to persuade people to join your religion or adopt your beliefs. ---
examples: Volunteers are told to help, not to proselytize.
He proselytized door to door for two years.
Staff complained about a colleague proselytizing at work.
entries.русский: обращать в свою веру, проповедовать; вербовать сторонников
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (they proselytized the whole village), intransitive (volunteers are told not to proselytize)

entries.meaning: To search an area for gold, oil, or minerals, or in sales to search for new customers. ---
examples: Crews still prospect for lithium in the desert.
His great-grandfather prospected for gold in Alaska.
The team spent the winter prospecting for new clients.
entries.contrast: Takes for: prospect for gold, not prospect gold.

entries.meaning: To do well, especially in money or business. ---
examples: Small shops prosper when the street is busy.
The family prospered after the war.
The company has prospered under new management.

entries.meaning: To make something last longer than it needs to. ---
examples: Do not protract the meeting with side questions.
Appeals protracted the case for six years.
The dispute has been protracted by both sides.

entries.meaning: To stick out from a surface. ---
examples: Rusty nails protrude from the old fence.
A rock protruded through the snow.
Wires were protruding from the wall.

entries.meaning: To examine someone's mind and motives by the methods of psychoanalysis, or informally to pick apart their behavior. ---
examples: Please do not psychoanalyze me at dinner.
The book psychoanalyzed three famous painters.
He spent the whole drive home psychoanalyzing his boss.
entries.contrast: The p is silent. American spelling is psychoanalyze; British writing uses psychoanalyse.

entries.meaning: To draw skin or cloth into small tight folds. ---
examples: Lemons make you pucker your lips.
The seam puckered after the first wash.
She was puckering her forehead at the screen.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (she puckered her lips), intransitive (the seam puckered)

entries.meaning: To blow out air or smoke in short bursts, or to breathe hard. ---
examples: The old engines still puff smoke over the valley.
He puffed on a cigar between innings.
She arrived puffing after six flights of stairs.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the chimney puffed smoke), intransitive (he puffed up the stairs)

entries.meaning: To vomit. ---
examples: Kids on that ride often puke.
The dog puked on the rug again.
He has been puking since midnight.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (he puked up his lunch), intransitive (the dog puked on the rug)
entries.contrast: Very informal. Vomit is the neutral word, and throw up the everyday one.

entries.meaning: To expand and contract, or grow strong and weak, in a steady rhythm. ---
examples: The lights pulsate in time with the music.
His whole hand pulsated with pain.
The floor was pulsating from the bass.

entries.meaning: To beat or move in a steady rhythm. ---
examples: Blood pulses through the vessels with every heartbeat.
The music pulsed through the floor.
A red light was pulsing on the dashboard.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the laser pulses light into the fiber), intransitive (blood pulses through the vessels)

entries.meaning: To crush something into powder, or to defeat it completely. ---
examples: The mill pulverizes the rock before it is washed.
The storm pulverized the old pier.
Their defense was pulverized in the second half.

entries.meaning: To move liquid or air with a pump, or to move something with that same in-and-out motion. ---
examples: These wells pump water all summer.
He pumped the brakes on the icy road.
Millions of gallons are being pumped into the reservoir.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (pump water from the well), intransitive (his heart was pumping hard)

entries.meaning: To blend food into a smooth, thick paste. ---
examples: Puree the soup in batches so it does not splash.
She pureed the carrots for the baby.
The sauce is made by pureeing roasted peppers.
entries.contrast: Both e's stay before the ending: pureed, pureeing.

entries.meaning: To get rid of people or things that are considered unwanted. ---
examples: New owners often purge the old management team.
The party purged its critics after the vote.
Old records were purged from the database.

entries.meaning: To remove dirt or harmful substances from something. ---
examples: Charcoal filters purify the water in an hour.
They purified the sample twice before testing it.
The air is purified before it reaches the lab.
entries.contrast: The -y becomes -ie in purifies and purified, but stays in purifying.

entries.meaning: To claim to be or do something, especially when the claim may be false. ---
examples: The emails purport to come from the bank.
The film purported to be a true story.
A document purporting to show the payment was leaked.
entries.contrast: The verb is stressed pur-PORT and is followed by to plus a verb; the noun purport (meaning) is stressed PUR-port.

entries.meaning: To draw your lips together into a tight round shape.
examples: Some people purse their lips when they concentrate.
She pursed her mouth and said nothing.
He listened with pursed lips.
